title: The artifact bundle format
purpose: Explain how artifacts on this site are packaged, so a consuming agent can interpret any bundle's intent, provenance and reliability before reading its contents.
summary: Each artifact is a directory of plain-text files with a JSON manifest. The manifest carries purpose, scope, method, confidence, load-bearing claims linked to sources and decisions, and a role for every file. Agents should read the manifest first and weigh content by its stated confidence.
audience: Agents and developers consuming artifacts from this site

excludes: The content of any particular artifact
How artifacts are researched or produced

method.summary: Designed from the questions a consuming agent has to answer before it can trust an unfamiliar document: what is this for, how was it made, how sure is it, and what did it deliberately leave out.
steps: Listed the questions a consumer needs answered before reading
Mapped each question to a manifest field
Aligned the site index with the llms.txt convention

limitations: Schema v1; fields may be added in later minor versions
open_questions: Whether claim-level provenance is worth its authoring cost on short artifacts

claims.statement: A consumer should read the manifest before any other file.
The site entry point follows the llms.txt convention.
Manifests are validated against a JSON Schema 2020-12 document published alongside them.
Version numbers follow semantic versioning, with a major bump meaning a conclusion changed.

sources.title: The /llms.txt file
sources.used_for: Shape of the site entry point

decisions.question: Should intent and provenance live in a separate manifest or in frontmatter of the main document?
decisions.rationale: Multi-file bundles need one place that describes every file. JSON validates against a schema and parses without a Markdown library.
decisions.dissent: Frontmatter keeps everything in one file and is easier to author for single-document artifacts.
alternatives: YAML frontmatter in the primary file
